newsitem.title: CANADA: Canadian T-bills open mostly weaker after CPI.
newsitem.headline: Canadian T-bills open mostly weaker after CPI.

text.p: Canadian T-bills opened mostly weaker on Tuesday in the wake of key Canadian and U.S. inflation data, as the two tame reports failed to boost prices, dealers said.

"There wasn't very good price action after the numbers came out. They were okay numbers for the market," said one T-bill dealer with a bank-owned brokerage. "Now the U.S. market is off a little bit more and we're feeling a bit heavy here."
Canada's three-month when-issued T-bill traded with a yield of 2.88 percent, unchanged from Monday's close.

Statistics Canada this morning reported core CPI in Canada in May rose 1.7 percent year-over-year, below expectations of a 1.8 percent rise. In the U.S., core CPI rose 0.2 percent in May from April, in line with expectations.
The Canadian money market is now focused on the auction this afternoon of C$4.3 billion in three-month, six-month and one-year T-bills. One dealer said the auction should draw decent interest.
"If we back up a little bit it should be okay. We don't expect it to be much of a problem," the dealer said.
In other prices, the six-month when-issued T-bill softened to yield 3.22 percent from 3.15 percent. The one-year T-bill softened to yield 3.66 percent from 3.63 percent.
The call loan or overnight lending rate traded at 3.0 percent, the center of the Bank of Canada's 2.75-3.25 percent target range.
